title: Cygnus (constellation)
description: Constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere
wiki_lead:
Cygnus is a northern constellation on the plane of the Milky Way, deriving its name from the Latinized Greek word for "swan". Cygnus is one of the most recognizable constellations of the northern summer and autumn, and it features a prominent asterism known as the Northern Cross. Cygnus was among the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy, and it remains one of the 88 modern constellations.
Cygnus contains Deneb, one of the brightest stars in the night sky, as its "tail star" and one corner of the Summer Triangle. It also has some notable X-ray sources and the giant stellar association of Cygnus OB2. One of the stars of this association, NML Cygni, is one of the largest stars known. The constellation is also home to Cygnus X-1, a distant X-ray binary containing a supergiant and unseen massive companion that was the first object widely held to be a black hole.
Many star systems in Cygnus have known planets as a result of the Kepler Mission observing one patch of the sky, an area around Cygnus.
Most of the east has part of the Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall in the deep sky, a giant galaxy filament that is the largest known structure in the observable universe, covering most of the northern sky.

History and mythology


In Eastern and World astronomy

In Polynesia, Cygnus was often recognized as a separate constellation. In Tonga it was called Tuula-lupe, and in the Tuamotus it was called Fanui-tai.  In New Zealand it was called Mara-tea, in the Society Islands it was called Pirae-tea or Taurua-i-te-haapa-raa-manu, and in the Tuamotus it was called Fanui-raro. Beta Cygni was named in New Zealand; it was likely called Whetu-kaupo. Gamma Cygni was called Fanui-runga in the Tuamotus.
Whilst being represented as a swan in the west, the constellation is known as ad-Dajājah in Arabic, meaning the hen. Cygnus's brightest star, known in the western world as deneb, gains its name from the Arabic name dhaneb, meaning "tail", from the phrase Dhanab ad-Dajājah or the tail of the hen.


In Western astronomy

In Greek mythology, Cygnus has been identified with several different legendary swans. Zeus disguised himself as a swan to seduce Leda, Spartan king Tyndareus's wife, who gave birth to the Gemini, Helen of Troy, and Clytemnestra, and Orpheus was transformed into a swan after his murder and said to have been placed in the sky next to his lyre (Lyra).
Later Romans also associated this constellation with the tragic story of Phaethon, the son of Helios the sun god, who demanded to ride his father's sun chariot for a day. Phaethon, however, was unable to control the reins, forcing Zeus to destroy the chariot (and Phaethon) with a thunderbolt, causing it to plummet to the earth into the river Eridanus. According to the myth, Phaethon's close friend or lover, Cygnus of Liguria, grieved bitterly and spent many days diving into the river to collect Phaethon's bones to give him a proper burial. grok_lead: Cygnus is a prominent northern constellation depicting a swan in flight along the plane of the Milky Way, recognized as one of the 88 official modern constellations delineated by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in 1922. It occupies an area of 804 square degrees, making it the 16th largest constellation and encompassing about 1.9% of the celestial sphere. Positioned in the fourth quadrant of the northern hemisphere (NQ4), Cygnus borders Cepheus to the north, Draco to the northeast, Lyra to the east, Vulpecula to the south, Pegasus to the southwest, and Lacerta to the west. Best observed during summer in the Northern Hemisphere, Cygnus culminates at midnight around late July and is visible to latitudes between +90Â° and -40Â°. The constellation is easily identifiable by its distinctive asterism, the Northern Cross, formed by five bright stars that outline the swan's wings and body when viewed upright, or the cross when tilted. This asterism, along with its position within the Summer Triangle âa large asterism comprising Deneb (in Cygnus), Vega (in Lyra), and Altair (in Aquila)âmakes Cygnus a key navigational feature in the northern summer sky. The brightest star in Cygnus is Deneb (Alpha Cygni), a white supergiant with an apparent visual magnitude of 1.25, marking the swan's tail and ranking as the 19th brightest star in the night sky. Its distance is estimated at 1,500â2,600 light-years; at the greater distance, Deneb has a diameter about 200 times the Sun's and shines with a luminosity roughly 196,000 times greater than the Sun's. The second-brightest is Albireo (Beta Cygni), a prominent double star at the swan's head with a combined magnitude of 3.1; it consists of a gold-hued giant and a blue companion separated by about 35 arcseconds. Other notable stars include Sadr ( Gamma Cygni) at magnitude 2.2, Gienah (Epsilon Cygni) at 2.5, and Delta Cygni at 2.9, all contributing to the Northern Cross. In Greek mythology, Cygnus is often associated with Zeus, who transformed into a swan to seduce Leda, wife of the Spartan king Tyndareus; their offspring included Helen of Troy and Pollux. Alternative myths link it to Orpheus, the musician turned into a swan after death, or to Cycnus, a mortal friend of Phaeton who drowned trying to retrieve his body from the Eridanus River and was immortalized as a swan by the gods. The constellation's name derives from the Latin for " swan," evolving from the earlier Greek designation "Ornithos" meaning "the bird." Cygnus is renowned for its wealth of deep-sky objects due to its alignment with the Milky Way's rich star fields. Key features include the Veil Nebula (NGC 6960, 6992, 6995), a supernova remnant about 2,400 light-years away spanning 3 degrees across the sky; the North America Nebula (NGC 7000), an emission nebula resembling the continent's shape; and the Pelican Nebula (IC 5070) adjacent to it. Open clusters like Messier 29 and the Cygnus OB2 association, containing some of the galaxy's most massive stars, further highlight its astronomical significance.
